Nathan Bellomy About [12,350] words
550 Jamaica Ave.
Brooklyn, NY 11208
nathanmcknight@gmail.com
(347)388-4953







Nellibeth
by Nathan McKnight









I could tell Poula was hiding something. I knew that look, that guarded play-it-straight look. I'd practiced for hours in front of the mirror trying to erase that same look from my own face. 
“So, you grew up right here on a cattle conservatory?” She gestured with hands covered in dirt. 
“More or less,” I said. “Gene's my uncle--we've always just called him him Unc. I think I was in the third grade when I moved in with him. Been ranching ever since.” I jammed the trowel into the ground and let my haunches settle into the dirt. 
“I like it,” she said. “I bet the woods are beautiful in the fall.” 
She had put a daisy behind her ear. The flower was a strange intruder against her pale-olive cheeks and coaly eyeliner. 
“So, you're going to buy it?” I asked.
“I wouldn't have spent the last hour helping you put in a flower bed if I wasn't going to stay and enjoy the flowers.” She made a sort of snurf noise that must've been a laugh. 
“You got a deal worked out with Unc?” She made a noncommittal head-shrug. Of course not, I thought. Unc would get my go-ahead before he did anything firm. “You don't much look like a rancher,” I said. 
Snurf. “Well. I raise animals sort of.” She stopped as if that were a satisfactory answer and looked down at her hands, awkwardly packing in a row of phloxes. 
I wanted to like her, but something triggered my suspicion reflex. I didn't think she was a sinkfarm scout--we'd had a handful of those come through already, wanting to strip the land, put in carbon repositories. She didn't seem right, but she didn't seem that sort of wrong. Their shiftiness usually had a missionary quality about it, trying too hard to make a good impression on everybody, not content with taking your land, they had to convince you of their holy mission too. Hers was much more of a skittish shiftiness.
“Look,” I said. “Me and Unc, we just want to see the ranch in good hands. While we've been running the conservatory here, we've always sheparded the land carefully. We let the wild plants and animals do their thing and we make sure the pastures and gardens don't dick up the wilderness too much. So, tell me what you've got planned and I'll tell you if we can do business. Unc'll back me up.”
She brushed the loamy soil off her hands and frowned. “Fair enough,” she said. And after another of her interminable pauses, she said, “Do you know much about...I guess you'd call it...meattech?”
I laughed out loud. “You've got to be kidding,” I said. 
“Look, if you don't want to--” But I cut her off.
“No, no. It's okay. Why didn't you just say so? Here I was thinking you were some kind of prospector.”
“Me? A prospector? Hardly.” She wiped her face with her wrist, leaving a smudge along her graceful jaw. “So...you're okay with me doing tissue engineering here?”
“Okay? Hell, we've been synthies for years. I would've showed you the vats in the shed, except that tends to scare away some buyers.”
“You do tissue engineering out here?”
“You can't not. I mean, we keep it to a minimum, but it's practically illegal to sell truly organic meats anymore.”
“And that doesn't bother you?” she asked with raised eyebrows.
“Mmmm--ten years ago, you might've gotten some argument from me, back when the regulations were first creeping in. It was a hard transition, especially for old-timers like Unc. But anymore, hardly a day goes by we're not taking core samples so we can tweak the mix.”
“Core samples? That's you call it?” She snurfed herself into a full-snort laugh. “Cow core samples? Ha! You're terrible.” 
She shook her head and scrunched her nose like I'd made a horrible pun, but a full-face smile split her lips and her dark eyes skewered me. 
I spread my hands and did a little head bow. “Glad to be of some amusement.” 
“So...you'll put in a good word for me with your uncle?”
“We'll see,” I said with a wink. 
“Well. Thank you. I'm glad we got that cleared up, but unfortunately it's about time for me to head back home,” she said. “Let me give you my card. I teach classes at Nutrielle. I'm not sure how applicable it would be for a ranch lab, or even if you want to keep up with tissue work after you sell the place, but if you're interested...”
“Moi?” I said, taking the card. 
After she rinsed her hands under the brittle old garden hose, she said, “I don't suppose I could bother you for a lift to the train station?” 
#
On the way back to the ranch, I kept thinking back to the smiles she gave me as we planted together. Poula was young, no more than about twenty, and maybe I was reading her wrong, but I swear there was something between us.
When I pulled back up the gravel drive, I saw the flowerbed she'd helped me finish. The front, where Poula had worked was precise, meticulous. In the back of the bed, along the barn wall, her neat ranks of peonies gave way to my free-form clots of lambs' ears and wildflowers. 
Unc was sitting on the astroturfed front steps, sipping soda from a juice glass. 
“Nice work,” said Unc, waving the glass at the flowers. “Although, your half's a little messy.”
“Ain't that the truth,” I said. “You're looking pretty rough yourself, old man.”
“That's 'cause I'm old. What's your excuse?”
I flipped the John Deere cap off his head when I walked in the door and chuckled as I left him cursing in the twilight. 
When I got inside, I examined the card she'd given me. It was a classy translucent white with a repeating threedi of a butter knife slowly slicing through a steaming fillet mignon. It read: 
Poula E. Santiban
Nutritional Tissue Consultant
Serving the Five Burroughs of New York
Teladdress: @SantaPoula2033
Scribbled on the back, in pen that made the animation fizzle and crack:
@NutrielleLLC
#
I left a message in Nutrielle's callbox as soon as I got inside, but my phone immediately chirped back an auto-reply telling me all the classes were filled. 
When Unc came in, clutching the hat, I wiped the frown off my face and asked, “How'd it go?” 
He made a humorless snort, and said “Well, it seemed like they might take the financial hardship claim seriously until her attourney brought up the fact that I'm selling the ranch. He'd printed off a bunch of those classifieds we took out. The judge said he'd consider the request again in six months.” 
“That's good news,” I said, trying to cheer him up. “All we have to do is not make the sale, then I'm sure he'll grant us an exemption and we can put it all behind us.” 
“Maybe,” he said, shaking his head. “But that's not the point. Y--we owe her,” he said, the frustration in his voice apparent. He should have said, almost did say: You owe her. 
I couldn't say anything to that, so I just said, “I'm going for a ride.”
“It'll be dark soon, Mac. Come on. What are you thinking?” 
“I know, I know. But that's just it. I have to do some thinking,” I said.
“You ain't been drinkin, have you?”
“Never touch the stuff,” I said.
“Uh-huh,” he said. “Go ahead then. I can't stop you.”
#
The spring air had cooled off, and I could see my breath and hers as I saddled and mounted old Nellibeth. I trotted her out to the tree-edge. 
Nellibeth knew the drill. She brayed and launched herself into the woods, arrowing between the trunks of the dewy oaks. Moon-stippled litter crunched underhoof as she deftly cantered over roots and rocks. She moved quick, and I had to hold my body hunched like a motorcycle racer to keep from getting hit by low-hanging vines. I didn't need to see where we were going. That was Nellibeth's job.
When Unc had first brought this beautiful brindled mare home from a 4-H meeting, I'd wanted to name her Nelly--after Nelly Square, who sang the theme to Adirondack & Quentin, my favorite twodi kidstoon at the time. Unfortunately, it happened to be the one weekend a month when my step-cousin, Rayne was visiting, and Rayne had thrown a hissy. For some reason, she'd wanted to call the horse Beth, and the two of us ended up in a muddy brawl over which one of us was Unc's real kid, even though we knew damn well he wasn't really either of our dads. 
Unc had split the proverbial baby and christened our new mare Nellibeth. 
The moonlight broke wide through the trees when we came upon the creek. The wild in Nellibeth broke out, as it always did. I loostened her reins and held tight to the gullet as she galloped through shallow water. The splashes gleamed, sparkling in the corners of my wind-watering eyes.
Nellibeth slowed after a time and grazed in a marshy sandbar. When I rode at night, I usually allowed my mind to wander where it would, and usually I allowed Nellibeth to lead the way. But tonight, it happened that Nellibeth was wandering away from the creek, starting to descend one of the numerous slopes towards The Way I Didn't Ever Want To Go Again; the path where I had my drunk horseback riding accident so long ago. It sounds funny to say it that way, but it's a serious matter. Serious as a dead cousin, sister, lover. 
I yanked the reins, and Nellibeth slowed her descent down the Oak Hill path until she was moving slow enough that I could turn her around. 
And as far as my mind was concerned, I didn't want to think about anything but the little animated card I'd left on my dresser, and the way Poula's dark eyes had pinned mine when she'd given it to me. 
#
As usual, Unc was sitting over the old threedi set when I got up, still in his longjohns. There was a Steelers game on, and he pounded his knee with the heel of his hand, sipping his a Budweiser straight from the pouch and yelling at the little players who faded in and out as they dashed across the worn metal screen. 
“A little early for a beer, don'tcha think?” I said.
“You're one to talk.” 
He leered at me as I plodded into the kitchen to make a pot of coffee. When I went to fill up the coffee machine's reservoir I saw that, out of habit, I'd left my phone on the sink window sill. Poor thing chirped plaintively because it wasn't getting enough sunlight there this late in the spring and the battery was about dead. 
I scrolled through my messages as the pot was brewing. Calls about the ranch had picked up. Most of the teleddresses were unlisted, probably scouts, so I reflexively deleted them. I didn't want to see the place go into a sinkfarmer's hands. A couple of the messages were private numbers, and I almost started listening to them just as the coffee maker finished dripping. 
Fuck it, I thought. 
“I don't want any y'all to have it,” I muttered and emptied my callbox, then poured myself a mug of coffee and had a breakfast of a couple spicy dill pickle spears and a week-old powdered donut. Afterwards, I went out to the shed. 
Our setup was just a little cubby with a fume hood and fan. There was a twodi screen sprayed onto the dusty wood, hooked up to a cracked glass pane for magnifying, but we never used them anymore. Marred by white scum, a small window afforded a view of “the Fleet,” as Unc called our herd, studding the hill behind the horse stable. We used to corral them up over the hill to the Knudsen's place for slaughter but Dale closed shop a couple years back and now we had to pay to truck them out to Oneida. I pulled the long syringe tips out of the dewar flask, noticing I'd need to head into town to top off the nitrogen soon.
Me and Unc didn't do much as far as tissue engineering was concerned, just seeding a few core samples with engineered cell lines and innoculating the cattle a couple times a year to keep their meat uniform and lean. I had only once made a batch of fully synth steaks. 
When he was gearing up for the switchover, Unc had first bought the wrong starter kit and we had a bunch of unused armatures and nutrient mixes laying around for a while. Eventually, I'd figured I'd give it a shot and see how they'd turn out. After a week's work, I'd had a gross of tenderloins ready for slicing. Unfortunately, they didn't turn out picture perfect like the ones stamped out by the millions in the industrial labs. We froze a couple to eat ourselves, and slapped the rest with an Artisinal label. They didn't sell that well, but at least it hadn't been a total loss. I snapped the cores onto the agar-loaded syringes and put them in the incubator. Tomorrow was the big day. 
A couple of the town boys who had helped us in the past were coming over to give us a hand wrangling the cattle, but we'd probably still have to drive over to the hardware store and pick up some day labor. It would be a good opportunity to top of the nitrogen.
I was lugging the dewar onto the bed of my pickup when Unc came running out, waving something in the air. 
“Mac!” he shouted. “Get over here. Don't make your old man run.” 
This was as excited as I'd seen him in years. 
I figured the Steelers must've won, but he panted, “It's that girl. Says she's been trying to get a hold a you all day. You shadowed your phone again, dint'ya? Anyway, she wants'ta make an offer but said she had to talk to you first.” He handed me the phone he'd been waving wildly, and jabbed a finger towards me, saying “You make sure this doesn't fall through. This is your recompense young man.” 
Poula? Trying to get a hold of me? I sat the dewar down and took the phone, shaking. I hadn't realized until that moment how much of an impression she'd made on me. I'd barely talked to a girl since Rayne passed away.
“Hi, MacElray?” she said. “So, I was glad to see you called about the classes. Your name's on my wait list for next semester, but I wanted to tell you...there's an opening in a special training class I'm running here for employees of one of our subsidiaries, and I figured since you already had some experience, you'd fit right in. They're all from different branches and they're all relative new-hires, so you could even audit the class for free and nobody would be the wiser.” 
“Um,” I was a little foggy-headed and I wasn't sure how to reply. 
“Sure, I guess. Yeah.” I said.
“Great. Show up at the Nutrielle building at eight sharp. You know where it is?”
“Wait, tomorrow?”
“Yeah, sorry. I forgot. That's the only catch. But this could be a really good thing for you. It might even be a foot in the door here or at BetaSynth, or wherever.”
“I wish I could, but I can't make it into the city tomorrow. We've got a lot of work lined up on the ranch,” I said.
“Oh, okay.” She sounded disappointed. “Well...think about it. If you show up, you're in. If not... Maybe some other time, I guess.” 
There was a long silence, then we both tried to speak at once. “Um...I was going to ask you to join me for dinner afterwards.”
“Wow,” I said, astonished. 
“Don't answer now. Just think about it, okay?” 
“Yeah,” I said. “Okay.”
Another long pause, then I said, “Unc says you wanted to make an offer on the ranch?”
“Oh, right. I, um...” And just then, the usual hesitation which I'd almost started to appreciate in her voice turned a corner and that skittish shiftiness came back. 
She said, “I'm not a hundred percent certain, but I, I think I can offer seven-fifty, with maybe twenty percent down. The thing is, I've got some...research and they're going to buy it and usually they pay so much and they really like my work and I've got a meeting lined up and...well, I should know in the next couple days.”
“Alright,” I said, again at a loss for words. 
“We'll talk about it tomorrow,” she said. “Either on the phone or, I hope, over dinner.”
#
1. Unc threw a fit when I told him I wanted to go into the city while he was here inoculating the Fleet. 
“What do you mean you're going to the city?” He said. “You can't leave me here to run the inoculation alone. I don't care how many extra hands we hire, I can't lead them all on my own. We don't keep the Fleet in shape, we don't make our money, we don't fix up the property, we don't sell the property. You don't get it. It's important, son.”
“That's why I'm doing it, Unc. That's why I'm going. Because she wants to buy the farm and she wants to talk about it over dinner,” I yelled. “Don't make it about me and you. So yeah, I'm going.” 
“Bull. Shit. What kind of dinner lasts all day long, MacElray? This ain't about the ranch, or she'da made a for real offer already. And this sure in hell ain't about you and me, Mac. This is about you. Just you. So, fine. Fine! Go.” 
I pushed over the dewar and let its contents sizzle out, sending ice-cold steam across the gravel.
“I'm takin the fuckin horse out,” I said.
#
This time, me and Nellibeth rode all the way down the creek to Oak Hill path and kept going. It was still early, and though my memories were crisp, the midday sun had the effect of washing out some of the pain. During the day, it was just a thing that had happened. At night...
I shook it off. I remembered the late steed Peanut Butter, after me and Rayne and Lizzie had ridden through the creek. The horses shaking off in the clearing here, sending water over the three of us. 
Me and Rayne used to sneak Budweisers out of Unc's fridge in the barn whenever she visited. Usually, the two of us got drunk and took turns daring one another to climb on the roof of the stable or run buck naked through the cow pasture. But Lizzie was younger, and when we offered her a Bud, she must've been afraid to touch the alcohol stash of a man who was, after all, a stranger to her. Rayne followed her friend's lead and I'd just figured more for me.
Night riding is always a blast, but the alcohol had raised the lid for me. It was ecstatic. When we broke out into the starlit creek, with stars made of water flying by on both sides, and real stars above reflecting in the water below...
It was like flying through space. 
After the horses shook off, we dismounted to wipe our faces with our hands and some kind of drunk humor made me want to fingerpaint with mud all over Nellibeth's flank—I think I'd been thinking something like, see if you can shake this off. Well, she shook alright. 
Lizzie got down, ducked right under Nellibeth. Stupid. Nellibeth sat right down on top of her, and although I heard the popping crack that might have been her collar bone, I hadn't recognized it for what it was, and I couldn't help but burst into laughter. Rayne had tried to pull her friend out, but Nellibeth had other plans. She rolled over, smashing Lizzie's face into the mud and knocking Rayne onto the rocks, unconscious. The mare had wiggled around on her back until she was satisfied she'd gotten all the mud off, then stood and trampled Lizzie as she ran off into the darkness.
Even in my drunken stupor, I knew better than to move Lizzie. She'd been broken up too bad. I didn't think to check if she was breathing. I just lugged Rayne onto Peanut Butter and rode back to the ranch as fast as I dared.
Me and Unc had left Rayne on the porch and called an ambulance, then we'd gone off on foot to get Lizzie. 
After I don't know how long hiking--all the while Unc muttering about how he should've put a goddamn lock on that goddamn refrigerator--we found the spot and when we shined a flashlight in Lizzie's face, we saw her mouth and nose jam-packed with mud. She was clearly dead. Until Rayne passed on after more than a year in and out of a coma, Lizzie was the only dead body I'd seen. She's still the one that haunts me.
The next day, we'd discovered that Peanut Butter had suffered a broken leg somewhere along the way. Nellibeth didn't turn up for three days. We'd found her grazing in the cow pasture, listless and bothered, but completely clean.
You'd be surprised at how much paperwork there is these days when a large animal dies, but me and Unc had gone through it all together, and I think it even brought us a little closer together. The other deaths, we didn't talk about.
I broke myself out of my memories, and let Nellibeth find her own way home. After I got her back into her stable, I made a call to Dale Knudsen's son, Rick. He agreed to give Unc a hand with the inoculation, waving off any notion of payment. Me and Ricky used to be buddies, and he'd spent plenty of time helping out here, not to mention working for years on his own dad's ranch. 
He'd be a more than a passable substitute for me. Besides, I think Unc was always fond of Ricky, so I figured they'd be happy to see each other again. I hoped that would take some of the sting away from my abdication. 
When I told Unc, he seemed satisfied, but said: “Alright, go to the class. But could you try to be back early enough to swing by Tanninger's for a nitrogen refill? The account's in your name, so I don't think me or Ricky can do that without you.”
I nodded and pulled on my dusty brown leather jacket. I stayed silent all the way out the door, my anger from the argument dulled but not forgotten. 
#
The Nutrielle building was a small shard of glass, lost among all the more famous spires of the Manhattan skyline. When I showed up, Poula checked me off on her list like the other few students who arrived at the same time, even asking my last name, though she must've known it perfectly well. 
“Welcome, Mr. Dresch,” she said in a professional tone. Only the barest hint of a smirk let me know that she even recognized me. 
In the classroom, Poula wasted no time.
“Okay guys,” she said. There was a dozen or so of us, and at thirty-five, I'm pretty sure I was the oldest. “You all have some experience or BetaSynth wouldn't have hired you, but I'm sure there's a wide range so let me know if I'm going too fast.”
The class was being held in a sterile white conference room covered in deactivated threedi screens. The room's only character came from a few scuffs on the floor and a plastic plate, knife, and fork at each seat. The plates each bore a beige paper cone, and I swear it looked like a we were preparing to eat dunce caps for breakfast.
“On the table in front of you,” announced Poula, “you'll find a sample of edible synthetic flesh. Go ahead and take a look. Smell it, touch it, taste it.” 
Poula's demeanor shocked me a bit. Her halting sentences and awkward intonations were gone and she spoke with a force and certainty beyond her years. It reminded me of the way Unc used to talk to me and Rayne when I we were young. I lifted the cover on my sample and poked at the synthmeat. It was pale, mushy. I cut off as thin a slice as I could manage with the tiny plastic knife and fork. 
“Don't eat too much now. You're sharing. Okay, so who thinks--” she started. 
The flesh in my mouth had a chemically, acrid flavor, so I raised my hand right away to tell her mine was the flawed sample. 
“I haven't even finished asking the question,” she said with her little snurf. “A little over-eager, are we? I was going to say, who thinks they have a good sample?”
I looked around, embarassed, but nobody else put up their hand.
“Good,” she said. “Every single one of these has something wrong with it. Too much EDTA, too little EDTA, not enough synth blood, too much fat, too long on the armeture, poor l-sally ratio.”
This isn't too bad, I thought. Nothing more complicated than the booklet that came with Unc's acidentally-purchased synth kit.
“Under each plate, you'll find a card listing the sample's vitals,” she said. “Taste them all, do a mental analysis, and see if you can figure out what causes the off flavors, colors, textures. Make a note of what's wrong with it and how you know what's wrong with it.” 
Suddenly, I realized I was in over my head. I'd just picked up what little I knew from the tiny booklets and instructional videos that came with the Unc's farm synth kits--more than anything, I'd thrown myself into learning how to keep our meat up to code to get my mind off Rayne and that little girl Lizzie. I didn't know thing one about analyzing synthmeat for biochemical flaws. 
But I didn't want to embarass myself, so I played hung in there as best I could. 
Poula went on, apparently off the top of her head, barely taking a second to breath between sentences.
“Learn to recognize the signs of an off batch. You won't want your instruments be a crutch once you get on the line. When you walk into a lab, if you aren't tasting your work, you aren't doing your job,” she said. “Eventually, you'll be able to tell a bad batch by tasting the agar. But to start, you should come to work hungry every day. Alright guys, now rotate and do the same thing with the next sample.” 
Poula lectured almost non-stop the whole morning. She didn't seem to pay me any special attention, even though I tried to catch her eye every chance I got. The class rotated and tasted, sniffed and took notes, and Poula made the rounds. Each time she came by my station, she nodded and carefully avoided my gaze.
“Now that you've ruined your appetite, I see it's lunch time,” she said finally. “Break.”
When the other students mingled and ate packed lunches, sinking into the cushy leather sofas in the building's lobby, I went to the restroom and made sure my collar was straight and my hair wasn't sticking up before perusing stiff portraits of Nutrielle executives while I waited to ask the receptionist where Poula's office was. 
I found her in her sixth floor office, eating sliced apples and dulce de leche and sitting crosslegged in a big swivel chair behind an even bigger threedi desk, surrounded by little plastic vats and boxes marked with chemical safety infomration. 
“So,” I said, hoping I sounded more jovial than insecure, “did you already forget me?”
“Of course not,” she said with a smile. “But I can't play favorites in class. Close the door.”
I did as she asked, now feeling overwhelmed by jittery anxiousness. She asked if I was enjoying the class, and I told her I thought she was phenomenal. Her cheeks turned five shades of crimson. 
“Take a look at this,” she said, kicking off the desk and riding the chair across to the full-wall window behind her. For a second, I thought she was going to fly through the glass and plummet to the granite sidewalk, but she stopped herself gently and reached down into a large paper-towel-lined aquarium on the floor. Delicately, she coaxed a tiny black mouse into her cupped hand, then wheeled back to the desk.
“Cute,” I said. “What's his name?”
“This is Percy-2,” she said. All at once, her tone dropped nearly to a whisper. It was that same strange skittishness, only more...conspiratorial. 
“I made him,” she said, petting with her pinkie between his translucent pink ears.
“What's that?” I wasn't sure I'd heard right. ”Did you say you made him?”
She just nodded, biting her lip and pegging me with her eyes. The confusion must've been plain on my face, so she went on.
“Look, you and I, we both make tissue, right? On the farm, in the lab, what's the difference?” she said with a shrug, then went on, “Nothing, except that I have more equipment, more reagents. So, I can grow...more tissue.”
“But how did you...” How do I say this? “...h-how did you...put him together?”
“Well, not that long ago, we used to have to make whole synthetic organ systems to keep our synthflesh alive, before we got the gist of the nutrient baths and stuff. So, I was practically synthing whole organisms from the start. The first time I tried really going all the way, with Percy-1, I had to grow most of the organs seperately, suture everything together. P-One wasn't perfect, but he wasn't Frankenstein's monster either.”
“But he didn't survive?” I asked.
“Well, he lived five and a half years...that's a really long time for a mouse.”
“But you didn't suture this one together?” I asked.
“Nope,” she said. “I grew him in situ, using normal armatures--the new ones that dissolve on their own. I had to go through quite a few test runs. Fifty or a hundred maybe. Most of those failed because the I didn't monitor the circulatory system or the nervous system development closely enough, but I got better with each try.
“Now,” she said, “I can make the whole integrated animal, nerves, muscles, capillaries, everything--for the most part...well...almost indistinguishable from the real thing unless you're looking closely with a good magnification screen.”
I reached out and pet the little thing. Not completely indistinguishable, I thought. Not if you know what you're looking at anyway. 
On first glance, the only strange thing about it was the violet eyes. The ears were beautiful, completely symetrical right down to the tiny veinlets. If you didn't know this mouse was synth nose to tail, you might not think much of it, the closer I looked, the more I could tell there was something weird about the little guy. Some parts were too perfect, others weren't quite right. Its legs were slightly stunted, its ribs bowed out too wide. 
“I love the eyes,” I said.
“They're my signature,” she replied in a whisper. 
Hushing her tone even further, as though she were speaking to the mouse, she said, “You can see I still have some trouble with the bones. Y'know, nobody's ever really tried to grow bones before, never needed to. I think I'm the first. I'm ready to move on to larger animals.”
Those last words were just mouthed, nearly voiceless. And I...well, I was speechless. 
“You're amazing,” I said, feeling a fizzling tingle run up my back and over my shoulders. 
Her lips parted as if to speak, and in that moment, I was more attracted to her than any other girl I'd ever met, seen, or imagined. 
A knock on the door broke my reverie. 
“Oh, hey Doug,” she said, waving somebody in. 
Feeling out of place, I stood and nodded curtly at the stranger. He was a slight fellow, with a slack face and etchglass spectacles. I hadn't seen a pair of eyeglasses actually in use for years; he must've been waiting for corrective surgery. He couldn't have been too poor--the suit he wore was obviously tailored for his lank frame. He didn't introduce himself, and he barely looked at me, so I gave Poula a wave and an awkward wink and went to let myself out.
“Before you go,” she said, leaning forward to hand me a glossy piece of paper, “here's a flier for the restaurant. Meet me after class?”
When I took the flier, I brushed her sleeve and noticed it was damp. I recoiled slightly, but immediately forgot the surprise when I felt my face break into a shy smile. It felt very, very good to allow myself a little joy after spending so long cooped up in my own private Purgatory.
“See you there,” I said. 
#
I managed to get through the rest of class without embarassing myself, and without fretting too much over Poula's aloofness. Her apparent fondness of me buoyed my confidence and carried me through. 
The flyer was a vidpaper scene of people laughing and using some kind of thin bread to scoop mush from a giant communal platter. Ras Kasar, it whispered in a sultry and accented androgynous voice, Finest Ethiopian cuisine. It didn't look all that appetizing to me, but when the video loop repeated and the food was again unveiled, the flyer emitted a rich, mouth-watering odor waft. 
I fanned my face for a moment, enjoying the savory scent, then tapped a corner tab marked Get Directions. The scene faded and an ornate arrow appeared, briefly swinging back and forth before settling on a direction and displaying a distance. 
The restaurant was a little under a mile away, and I spent the walk racking my brains to think of something to talk about besides the twin elephants in the room: Her offer on the ranch, and that mouse of hers. 
When I arrived, I was greeted by that same voluptuous scent and I told the maitre d' I needed a table for two. Poula was nowhere to be seen, and I couldn't resist the urge to check my appearance again, so I tossed my jacket over the little stool that the thin, jet-skinned young man led me to, and found my way down a mirror-wallpapered corridor to the restroom. I couldn't believe how giddy I was getting. In my excitement, I bumped a waiter and got something with a sweet buttery-spicy smell on my shirt. 
The stain paled and widened with the wiping and I cursed my clumsiness as I daubed my sleeve with a wet paper towel. I was preoccupied enough that I didn't notice the stranger come in and stand next to me.
Finally, the stranger said, “You wouldn't like Poula as much as you think you would.” 
I jerked my head up to see a dog-faced man with glasses in profile. His age seemed indeterminate, very youthful, but somehow worn. I guessed he must've been a teenager, cursed with unusually bad teeth and skin. He looked profoundly sad.
The boy stared forwards so that I could only make eye contact by looking a him in the mirror. Even if it weren't for the archaic etchglasses, I would've recognized his distinctive slouch, those droopy-joweled cheeks. 
“Excuse me?” I said, instinctively dropping into Unc's authoritative twang.
“She's better off alone,” he said, with a sad tone. 
Through my confusion, I mustered a reply: “Don't you think that's for...her to decide?” 
“No,” said the boy plainly. 
He turned, and when he pulled the restroom door open, I saw that his hand didn't open all the way and he walked with a limp. 
“You'd be better off leaving her alone,” he said as he departed.
“What the hell is that supposed to mean?” I spat. 
But the boy was gone and the door thwacked shut leaving an echoing silence in its wake. I tried to shake offf the weird encouter and I cleaned my sleeve as best I could. Finally, I just rolled up my sleeves and hoped the stain wouldn't be too noticable.
Poula had found the tiny wicker table and sat on the stool across from my jacket. 
“I ordered a sampler for two,” she said as I sat. “I hope you don't mind.”
“No problemo,” I said, wondering if I should bring up the kid in the bathroom. “I've never had Ethiopian. Hell, I didn't even know they had food in Ethiopia,” I said. When she didn't laugh, I tried to make my comment seem more serious, saying: “You know, what with the war and all?”
She said nothing, just wiped her hands with the steaming towel that had been placed in front of her while I was up. I shrugged, then followed suit with the towel in front of me. It was piping hot, and while I wiped each finger, I tried to remember if I had figured out anything to talk about, but I came up empty.
“Just think,” she said, breaking the silence. “A week from now and you'll have a Level-A Nutrielle E.S.T. Certificate.”
“You're going to certify me? I thought I was just auditing the class,” I said. 
She shrugged and said, “You're welcome.”
“What should I tell them if they ask about BetaSynth?” I asked. 
She considered briefly, then: “I don't think there's anyone here from the Trenton office, so tell them you're a brand new lab assistant there--you got hired over the phone and you haven't even set foot in the facility yet. Beyond that, the truth should work out alright, MacElray.”
She stumbled over my name, pronouncing it Mick-el-ray.
I chuckled, and said, "It's pronounced Mackle-Ray.”
"Mack, El Rey," she repeated dramatically, and snurfed in that adorable way she had. 
"Good enough," I said. 
The waiter set up a tray next to us and layed out a veritable blanket of spongy bread, letting the stuff drape over the edge of the table like a tablecloth. He dished out half a dozen thick stews and poured us each a glass of golden wine. 
Poula made a dainty silent clapping motion, then pinched off a spongy bit of bread and held it up to her six-sizes-too-big peacoat. To my surprise, a tiny pair of hands and whiskered nose yanked it into the darkness of an inside pocket. 
“Percy?” 
She nodded in answer.
“You're something else,” I said. 
“How do you feel about going into the industrial side of the business?” she asked.
“Not sure. It does seem like that's where the money is.”
She shook her head. 
"No," she said. "The money is in niche markets, natural meats. If you're looking for money, stick with cattle conservation." 
"I can think of one reason I might want to change fields," I said, nervously reaching towards her hand.
I trained my eyes on hers, followed those dark pearls as they scanned down my arm, watched me put my hand in hers. 
For a tense moment, she seemed astonished. 
Then, she closed her fingers around mine and glanced around as if we might be caught in a scandal. I stifled a giggle, but she giggled outright and for that instant, it felt like we were two schoolkids getting ready to make out behind the barn.
The warmth of her touch was electrifying. 
We ate the rest of a fantastic meal, made all the more wonderful by the mingling of flavors and smells and touches and the quiver of coursing emotions. She told me about how her in situ techniques had caught the attention of some of the higher-ups at Nutrielle and how they'd casually mentioned their compensation for certain much less groundbreaking patents had been three-quarters of a million dollars. She said she'd know for sure in a couple more days, and asked if anybody else were looking at the place. 
“I doubt anybody else would make such a generous offer,” I said, knowing it hardly mattered. I wanted Poula to buy the conservatory, at any price. I wanted to see her use my ranch to achieve her dreams. 
“So, who was that guy who came into your office today?” I said. 
“What, Doug?”
“Yeah, he gave me a pretty cold stare back there in that office.” I didn't want to alarm her, so I didn't tell her about the encounter in the bathroom. 
“Did he?” she snurfed, and said “Don't worry about Doug. He's a veep at Nutrielle, so he thinks he owns everybody and everything.”
“Does he think he owns you?” 
For a second, I thought back on the execs' portraits in the lobby at Nutrielle, but none of the faces I remembered looked like Doug. The youngest of them'd looked to be in their forties. 
“Nobody owns me,” she said. Then, “We had a thing a while back, but it was nothing. He's an idiot.”
“Sorry if I'm prying, I guess I just kinda assumed you liked older guys,” I said, pointing my thumbs at my chest with a wink.
She laughed out loud, and said, “You assumed right,” then she leaned across the table and wiped away my concerns with a sensuous kiss, “and please, don't get too self-conscious about your age.”
Too soon, she said, "I should probably get back to work," as she untangled her hand from mine. “If you don't mind picking up the bill, I'll get dinner tomorrow,” she said with a wink.
I nodded and smiled, and she departed with a very un-Poula-like bouncy gait. 
"See you in class," I said as I beckoned the waiter to pack up the leftovers.
#
It was a long drive back to the ranch, and the glow from that amazing dinner slowly faded while the Sun nestled in behind the Pallisades. As my emotions returned to level, it gradually dawned upon me that I'd broken my promise to Unc.
When I got back home, it was completely dark but for the light in the kitchen window. 
Bursting in the door, I said, “I'm so sorry, Unc. I forgot about the nitrogen but I have good news...”
“Don't worry about the nitrogen, Mac. I have to tell you something,” he said. 
Apparently, one of the hired hands had done something to spook the Fleet when they were moving them to the barn.
Unc delivered the news solemnly, saying “The Fleet ain't that big, but a little stampede is still a stampede. I was on horseback, and when they came at her, Nellibeth threw me. I'm okay, but she took off through the woods. We tracked her and found her at the bottom of the gully on the far side of Oak Hill.”
I put my head in my hands, and took a shuttering breath.
“Ricky says he don't mind comin over in the mornin to help dredge up the body,” said Unc.
I was in shock, I wanted to tell him I was sorry, but he was the one who was apologetic. He knew how close I was to Nellibeth. I suspect he even had an inkling that I saw her as my last connection to Rayne.
“At least no people were hurt,” I said.
“Ain't that the truth,” he said, taking a long breath and looking older than I'd ever seen him. 
When I finally told him about Poula's upcoming offer, he just shrugged with a slight nod. 
#
In the morning, I hiked down to the gully to pay my respects to Nellibeth. The sight of her bloody body, legs all twisted in different directions at the bottom of the scree haunted me the whole way into the city. 
Though I'd gotten up at the crack of dawn, I still ended up twenty minutes late to class, and when I came in, Poula said, “You got lucky, we almost went to the training lab without you.”
That day, and for the following two days, we were all paired up with lab partners and stationed at fume hoods not unlike my old shed lab back at the ranch.
My lab partner was a boy named Scootch, only a tad younger than Poula, but much more immature. He asked lots of questions of me and Poula both, but after a couple days re-explaining things that had already been explained ad nauseum, he grew tiresome for both of us. When he told me he liked me because I had a name weirder than his, I stopped talking to him altogether and gave him the cold shoulder as much as possible. 
Next to Scootch, I felt like a lot less of a dunce, and once we got our hands on the practice gear, I felt more comfortable still. The preformed armatures were a little more sophisticated than the ones I'd used on those “Artisinal” beef loins, and they had to bathe in a more precisely controlled nutrient bath, but otherwise I was on familiar ground.
Submerge for thirty seconds while the cell-laced gel warms to body temperature, check nutrient levels, spread the gel onto the armature making sure the layers are as thin as the magnifying screen can resolve. Using tiny electroshock treatments, we'd whip the little sons-of-bitches into shape, developing nice meaty striations. Here and there, you had to inject a few globules of fat cells. The last step was to vacuum inject pre-packaged synthblood. 
“To make the meat acceptable to even a not-so-discerning-palate,” said Poula. Like Unc, I thought, ”the mix of textures and chemical constituents has to be balanced just so.”
For most of the students--and I still hadn't decided, but maybe, just maybe, for me too--this was the precursor to overseeing a thirty-thousand unit line. 
Me and Unc buried Nellibeth's carcass in the clearing at the end of Oak Hill path, and somehow that lightened the feeling of the place for me. It was still melancholy, and now that Nellibeth was gone, the major work of the season was done--and not by me--not to mention the impending sale...well, it felt like everything was coming to an end. 
But at the same time, it was a new beginning. 
Poula and me'd had dinner at a different restaurant of her suggestion each night after class, at a Tibetan place on Tuesday, and on Wednesday at a place where everything-but-everything was deep-fried. She still hadn't gotten word about the patent, but she assured me Nutrielle would be forking over an advance any day now.
Each night was capped off by long conversation in my pickup truck's cab in the Nutrielle parking garage, followed by a series of long, passionate kisses and a clumsy make-out session. I'd told her all about Nellibeth and Rayne, and Nellibeth's sudden death, and she nodded understandingly when I told her I couldn't talk about the accident. 
She'd told me stories of growing up a shut-in, sheltered by her father in one of the biggest Dominican enclaves in Brooklyn. We swapped jokes and sometimes she'd get drunk while I dutifully saved myself for the drive, and each night, she'd send me on my long drive home to replay the evening's high points in my head. 
#
By Thursday, I was champing at the bit. 
We were in my pickup, her silky lips nipping at my ear, my hands caressing her breasts, her fingers wandering over the muscles of my arms, my stomach, moving downwards and sliding deftly into my jeans. I would have pushed her back, unzipped her hoodie, and taken her right then if it wasn't for the damn gear shift. 
“It's a three-hour drive back home,” I sputtered between heavy breaths. “I don't suppose, I could...I'd sleep on the couch if you want.”
“It's not that,” she said. “It's just...it's kind of...messy.”
“I don't mind,” I insisted. 
I understood messes, I told her. Before I moved in with Unc, I'd lived in a house where hiding the dirty dishes in the stove was considered an acceptable way to straighten up. Letting an outsider into your own private squalor took trust.
“You can trust me,” I said.
“It's not like that,” said Poula, “I just...I just can't.”
And I spent the drive home that night pounding on the dash and trying not to let my shifting hand rub my insensed member. 
Unc'd left the kitchen light on as was his habit even when I wasn't gonna be out late, but the ranch was eerie silent, especially without the occasional snort and ppprrrur sound from the stable.
That night, I dreamt I was working with a partner in the old shed lab. It was Scootch, but it looked like the bathroom boy...what was his name? Dave? Doug? Enormously magnified images of muscle fibers and bones played across the again-functioning magnification screen, and we both had our hands in the agar, working and working and working for what seemed like forever. When we finally looked down at our creation, it turned out to be a disembodied human hand working its fingers open and closed and open again. 
#
The next day, Poula took the class to see a working synth line operation. The set-up was something different altogether from my shed lab or the class's practice hoods. 
She sat down behind a broad desk, whose surface was little more than a rotating view of its thirty-thousand units, divided in half and overlain on one another, so that any irregularities would be easy to spot. 
Each unit had a chromo display in the corner, and I was surprised to realize I'd learned enough this week to make sense of most of the display. When the chromo read too blue, it meant there were too little nutrients. Too white, the agar was too thin. Too orange, too thick. 
One by one, Poula asked us questions round-robin style. Even Scootch got most of them right.
As it turned out, grids 78-89 through 206-07 were running slow and a little alkaline.
“So boys, what do we do about this?”
“Where's the supply locker?” I asked.
As soon as she pointed, without missing a beat, we all got together and loaded up a cart full of EDTA and l-saliphrene. With a box cutter, I slashed the EDTA packets open and Scootch filled up a big 5000-mil flask at the lab sink. I mixed a smaller flask of acidified water and l-sally tablets. 
With help from the rest of the class, we added the reagents to the appropriate rows of the grow tables and re-calibrated the chromos against standard samples. 
“Bravo,” said Poula with a little prayerful clap. “Class-A Certificates all around!” 
“Thanks to the teacher,” I said, and when I realized I was in love and didn't care if anybody knew it, I added: “I told you you're amazing.” 
#
“So, what'll it be today,” I asked, gently laying my crisp new certification on the driver's seat and locking the pickup, “Vietnamese, Portuguese, manitees?”
“Well,” said Poula in a whisper, “in honor of your graduation, I had something special in mind.”
I felt tingles all over my body as animal lust began to well in my chest, but just as soon as it started, she threw cold water on my hopes, saying “It's just a little project I'm working on.” 
I tried not to let my discouragement bleed through and feigned curiosity as I let her lead me by the pinkie out the parking garage and down the street. There, she coded into a building with an old-fashioned camera and keypad security system.
We walked up two flights of stairs, where she told me to wait in the hall while she straightened up.
“It's my special lab,” she said.
After she disappeared through one of the many nondescript doors, I wandered to the stairwell window and looked out over a little park with a sparse collection of trees and a run-down dog run. There was a couple making out on a bench, and a guy limping along with a shopping cart full of plastic bags having an animated conversation with a mounted police officer. “Hey,” said Poula, making me jump. “You can come in now.”
I turned to see her standing in the doorway in translucent black bra and panties, and a fog of desire overcame my senses as I put my hands on her bare waist and nuzzled her neck, letting the sweet musty odor of her skin encompass me. She pulled me inside, and I was surprised to see it was just an ordinary apartment. 
“So this is your lab, eh?” I said. “You tricked me.”
If I'd've been less preoccupied with Poula's sultry curves, the fringe of peach fuzz around her navel, her pouty lips... I would have been surprised that the apartment wasn't messy in the least. There was a slight acrid odor, and I wondered if she owned a dog, but I couldn't follow that line of thought as she pulled me inside and shut the door, pinkie-leading me to her bed.
Our lovemaking was quiet and intense. The window at the headboard was open and moist air washed over us, cooling my sweaty skin, raising goose bumps on her Poula's creamy thighs. As afternoon became evening, the daylight reddened, sending pools of shadow over the sheets and painting our skins with glints of orange and gold. Poula sighed, a long cooing noise, the heat of sex drained from my body with a rush as I orgasmed, and Poula's goose bumps spread to my own skin. 
As soon as I could muster my muscles to move me, I stood to close the window, not caring whether the dog-walkers and cops got a good view of my nakedness. The wood was moist and swollen, and I had to stand up and put all my weight on the sash just to get it to budge. 
The smell of sweat was heavy in the air. 
The carpet was moist, and it sapped the warmth from my toes, so I crawled back under the covers and spooned Poula. She mmmmmed and cozied her buttocks against my crotch and I tucked her body under my arm, letting my forearm nestle between her breasts and my fingers caress her clavicle. In moments, I slipped into an amazingly comfortable stiff-cocked slumber. 
We both slipped in and out of sleep, punctuating the silence with sleep sighs and occasional quiet musings.
“Ever ride a horse through the forest at night?” I asked her. “It's amazing. Terrifying. Like flying through space.”
“I never rode a horse,” she said. “But I will I hope. It sounds dangerous.”
I told her about Rayne and Lizzie, reluctantly at first, but once the words came, they seemed to drain my soul, pouring out of me in a feverish whisper, my voice turning gravelly, like Unc's. I told her everything except the one detail I couldn't bear to admit--that I had been drunk. 
I couldn't tell you why I did it, I should have just said I didn't want to talk about it, but when it came to the fatal moment, I hesitated for a long moment, too long.
Then I said: “Rayne must've been drinking; she started rubbing mud on the horse, and I guess Nellibeth was trying to rub it off when she rolled over on top of Lizzie.”
#
In the morning, I opened my eyes to diffuse morning light shining through the window at the head of Poula's bed. The glass'd steamed up in the night and drips of water dotted the window sill. I tossed aside damp bedclothes and put my bare feet down on dewy carpeting. No wonder it smelled like she had a dog. There must've been mildew creeping into every crack and crevice in the place. 
Brushing aside annoyance, I tiptoed to the bathroom, which I found at the end of a short hall by the front door. There was another door, which might've been a closet, covered with a blue tarp that seemed to breath, as though somewhere behind there, it was open to the outside. 
I used the pot, and on the way back to bed, discovered the source of the apartment's pervading moisture. At the foot of the bed, a humidifier had been left running all night. I couldn't find the switch, so I unplugged the thing and, deciding I'd slept long enough, I started poking around. Poula was still snoring lightly under pink paisly covers. There wasn't much to it, just a tiny bedroom adjoined to an even tinier kitchen. 
My curiosity took a back seat to my zombie drive for coffee, and soon I was poking around the kitchen. Not even instant? I thought. The cabinets were empty and, aside from a half-full five pound bag of agar powder, so was the fridge. 
Poula still hadn't roused. That's why I'll never care for city life, I thought. Wreaks havoc with your body's schedule. 
Coming up empty on the coffee front, I reluctantly went back to bed, trying not to disturb Poula's sleep. Now that I'd noticed the doggy smell, I was having a hard time not noticing it. I laid awake for what seemed like hours, tracing patterns of water stains on the ceiling with my eyes. 
I must've dozed off eventually because before I knew it, I was roused again by a tap on the window. I half-dreamed the sound was the cracking of collarbone against stone, and just as fast as I was out, I jerked wide awake. I held frozen, senses buzzing alert, heart trying to punch its way out of my chest. 
“What the hell,” mumbled Poula, sleepylipped.
“Shhhh...” I said, wiping a clear swath across the cold, wet pane. 
The park was empty, except for one figure, on the sidewalk directly across the street, and even though he was distorted by the veins of water on the glass, I recognized bathroom boy, with his big glasses and twisted legs. His upraised arm dropped and I figure he must've seen me, because he turned and started walking away and I thought, Kid, you better walk away.
I muttered, almost inaudibly, “I'm not even fuckin joking,” and I wanted to disassemble that brat.
“What is it?” Poula whispered. 
“Nothing,” I said. “It's nothing.” 
But my fists were working open and shut, wondering if I'd really scared him off. I slid out of bed and into my now-damp clothes as quickly and quietly as I could. I let myself out and steeled my nerves for a confrontation.
Downstairs, I glanced back and forth, crossed the street and looked across the park. The place was empty but for a young girl exercizing an enormous mastiff in the dog run. I loostened my fists, deflated and turned back towards the apartment.
Sure enough, bathroom boy was there, huddled in a darkened doorway a couple doors down from Poula's place. I sprinted across the street, and grabbed him by the shoulder. 
He was obviously startled, and he yammered until I said, “Listen to me.”
He wore a loose jogging suit, and I had to twist the kevlon jacket around my hand to hold him still.
I told him, “Look,” I said, “I get it. I do. Nobody likes to lose a girl. I understand that better than anybody, but you need to stop this. You need to leave her alone and let her make her own decisions. And if you can't do that on your own...“
He hesitated a second. The dull eyes behind those glasses searched my face, then he straightened his demeanor and said, “Get your hands off of me, boy. I'm your boss's boss's boss, so ” 
His voice wasn't a kid's voice. He growled with as much gravity I'd seen in a man his age, sounded like Unc more than anything.
I thought it'd be better not to tell him I wasn't one of his employees, so I just said, “I don't care who you are. If you wanna get in her good graces, you're goin about it all wrong way.”
He shook his head, not vigorously, in defiance--but in what seemed like pity. 
“You should thank me,” he said. “Look at me. Poula made me like this.” 
He waved his hand over his body, his hunched back, his bowed legs, his wonky blue eyes. 
“She changed me,” he said. “And I tried to change for her. I did change for her. And then she left me. So go ahead, go back to her and just wait. She'll leave you like she left me. The only difference is, she doesn't need you. She needs me.”
The sudden change in this little boy--this man--made me take a step back, literally. I didn't know what to say, hadn't even quite absorbed all he'd said. 
He sneered and backed away, and I heard Poula's voice, turned, and he was gone. 
“Mackle Ray,” I heard. “Mackle Ray! What are you doing out here?” 
She was wrapped in a paisly bedsheet toga, and she leaned out the glass door as far as she could without moving her feet from the tile inside. I turned, glancing once more quickly around, then followed her back up the stairs and into the apartment. I winced at the bitter-tart odor, but she dropped her wrapping and pressed her nakedness against me.
“Does that Doug guy throw rocks at your window often?” I asked. 
“Oh Christ,” she said, and then she started what sounded like an apology
I interjected: “I don't think he'll be bothering you again.”
“You're so sweet,” she said, rubbing a her head against my neck and running a hand through my hair. “...and muscular.”
“Workin on the ranch ain't all bad, huh?” 
She giggled and we rushed back to bed.
#
“Well, I have to say--that was the best surprise you could have given me,” I said, all thought of Doug long behind me. 
“Oh,” she said, snurfing, “but that wasn't even the surprise.”
I raised my eyebrows and she went on: “I wasn't kidding when I said I wanted to show you the project I've been working on.”
“Come on,” she said, bouncing on the bed. “Let me show you my special laboratory.”
We got out of bed, both of us still naked, and walked across the wet carpet towards the bathroom, down the hall. 
I was confused, and my face must've showed it, because she put her finger on my lips as if to say shhhhh, then smiled. “It's okay,” she said.
She pulled back the blue tarp from the door in the hallway and a blast of sharp, cheesy odor nearly gagged me.
“Sorry about the smell,” she said. “I hardly notice it anymore. I just don't have proper ventilation here.”
The door opened onto a walk-in closet filled with...well, I couldn't tell at first what I was looking at. The first thing I identified was another little dome-shaped humidifier. The rest was a wet, tangled mess.
She bent and lifted a tile covered in a yellowy gel that took me a second to recognize as agar. She snapped it neatly into place on the wall, saying “Four hundred pounds of agar doesn't go as far as you might think.”
The whole closet glistened urea-yellow, and there was big globs of meat--whole, flexing muscles fastened down with straight pins and stretched out with zip ties. There was a pair of lungs, billowing open and closed. Everything was netted in a fine mesh of veins and a delicate tracework of white lace that must've been nerves. All of it writhed and pulsed, and it slowly dawned on me what I was looking at. 
Succored by the nutrient mixture, the wall was a whole living creature, splayed out like a diagram. 
Was this... and as the thought formed in my head, Doug's words came back to me, and my skin prickled. Was this...Doug-2? I couldn't get the sound out of my mouth, my stomach heaved. 
“What, wh...” I babbled incoherently.
“You'll find out,” said Poula. “That's the surprise.”
“What is it?” I finally said.
“Think about it, you'll figure it out,” she said. 
Sprigs of tendon and sinew sparkled along the tiles, muscles flexed, lungs billowed and collapsed like ship's sail in a strong wind. She picked up a spray bottle and spritzed a huge pair of discarnate, violet eyeballs, then snurfed. 
#
I left in the afternoon, giving her an unfeeling kiss. After she'd showed me the lab, we hadn't talked. It took me a long time to let it sink in. She's building another Doug, the thought had just kept going through my mind. She'd acted coy, like my confusion was funny, and that'd just made it worse.
The ride back home was frought with nightmare visions that the daylight failed to wash away. I smacked the seat, punched it harder and harder, cursed and eventually I just cried, driving home by feel when the tears blurred my vision too much to see. 
By the time I got home, my tears had dried, leaving powdery trails down my cheeks. I realized Doug was right. She doesn't need me, I thought. She needs him. 
The thought pierced my heart like a straight pin, and I gritted my teeth to stop myself from crying again.
Unc tried to get me to talk at first, the unnatural silence of the ranch echoing between his words. Eventually, he gave up and turned on the threedi to watch a game stoically. 
I didn't call Poula back. 
#
For a few days, I tooled around the ranch house, watching threedi and draining pouches of beer. Unc put up with my sulking for almost a week before he asked me to take the dewar for a refill.
The trip to the store helped my mood a little, and when I got back, I went to work feeding the cattle and cleaning the stable out one last time. By sunset, I was almost feeling normal and I even joined Unc for a Steeler's game. 
The phone rang that night, just as I was laying down for bed. It was Poula. I didn't answer and I almost deleted the message but, like prodding at a fresh wound, I couldn't stop myself from pushing play. 
Her voice was small. 
“I'm sorry that I upset you. I want to give you time, whatever you need. I love you, and I wish...” she trailed off. “The only reason I called is to tell you I didn't get the advance from Nutrielle. Their lawyers say they already own the patents because I worked for them when I made them. They just gave me a two thousand dollar bonus and recommended me for an honorary doctorate. It's bullshit. I don't know what I'm going to do, but I still want to buy the conservatory. I think if I talk to Doug--”
I hung up and went to bed.
#
The next morning, the full brightness of the sun was shining in my window as I tossed and turned, but I couldn't will myself to get out of bed. I sobbed into my pillow, trying to keep Unc from seeing my useless state, but he interrupted my pillow-drowned darkness with a nock on the door.
“You look bad,” he said.
I shrugged, then sat up with the sheets pulled over my shoulders.
“I just had a long conversation with Poula,” said Unc. “She was grilling me about you.”
“She's here?” I sputtered.
“Over the phone.”
I wasn't sure if I was feeling relief or disappointment, but I nodded and asked, “What did you tell her?”
“I didn't tell her nothin. We talked about the ranch, and told me she had the funds and wanted to buy it.”
“You're selling it to her?” I said with a dead flat tone.
“We'll talk about that,” he said. “The thing is...she asked about you and Rayn's accident. She told me you said Rayne was the one who'd been drinkin.”
I closed my eyes.
He went on, “It didn't occur to me that you would lie about such a thing, so I didn't even think to try to back up your little fib. I don't mean to hurt you, but I just told her what happened as best I knew it.”
I took a deep breath.
“What did she say?” I asked.
“Nothin. Not for a long time, then she said she had to go.”
Unc waited for me to say something, but when I kept the silence, he said: “I accepted her offer. It's not as much as she thought she was going to offer, but it's enough for me to buy a little house maybe. Probably not enough to pay our--your--debts.”
#
Poula came out with her lawyers to finalize the purchase with us and our lawyers, and I managed to drag myself out of bed and look presentable. 
I was surprised to see they came in three separate vehicles, with a horse trailer in tow. I wished I'd been surprised to see bathroom boy get out and stand alongside Poula.
She introduced her three lawyers, and we introduced our one. 
Finally, she said, “And you know Doug.”
“Shouldn't you say, Doug-1?” I asked, bitterness clinging to my teeth.
It couldn't have come as a surprise that I knew, but she looked confused. 
“Did you finish Doug-2 yet?” I spat.
She still shook her head, and I said, “He's obviously one of yours. Did you sew up that Frankenstein thing in your closet, or was it another failed experiment?”
Doug looked back and forth between us, then I saw him tilt his head back, forming his lips into an 'O' of recognition. 
“Stop,” he said. “No. Poula didn't make me.” 
He almost laughed--incredulous snurf, but not the adorable sound Poula made. 
“I made myself like this,” he said. “I used her techniques, but I did it myself...to look younger. I know it's wrong to blame her. I was mad. But it's my fault, not Poula's.”
Poula stood agape.
“You thought I made Doug?” she said. “Jesus, Mac. Oh my god, no, no, no...”
The herd of lawyers stood by like they were trying not to interfere with a barroom brawl.
“Then what was that monster in your closet,” I said.
“I was going to start with a cow, but you inspired me. It was supposed to be a surprise, like I said,” she said. 
She tapped Doug on the shoulder, pointed over her own shoulder. He nodded and went around back of the trailer. 
“She won't be perfect,” said Poula. “There aren't vats big enough, so I had to make her the old way. But at least Nutrielle--” she gave a sour glance to the lawyers. “Nutrielle is going to set up a new lab, right here. I'll be able to put my techniques into production.”
Doug backed a horse out of the trailer, walked it around, awkwardly. He obviously had never handled a horse before, but they made a good pair, him with his glasses and bent back, and the horse...well, she was beautiful. Her ribcage was a little wide, and her ears were too perfect. But her eyes were beautiful violet. 
Poula said, “I was going to name her Nellibeth-2.”
# 
“So,” I said, “that's how I got into edible tissue engineering. The judge ended up awarding Lizzie's family almost twice what Doug Lenzler bought the ranch for. I can't let my uncle pay that on his own, and that's why I'm looking for work. I see her on the threedi a lot, so I guess Poula must be doing well.”
I leaned back in the reclining chair and spread my hands in a there-you-have-it gesture.
The guy behind the desk looked slightly agog, and when he regained his composure, he said “I appreciate your honesty, MacElray. We'll message you in a few days to let you know our decision.”
As I stood, he added, “I can't begin to understand how you must feel about her, but having Dr. Santiban's name on your resume puts you way ahead of the crowd. Good luck.”

Yes. And I think the important distinction is that what you want is **not a story generator** in the usual sense. It is closer to a **deterministic constraint-preserving transformation system over a narrative graph**.

No statistical approximation is necessary.

The abstraction we made can be represented as a typed graph:

\[
\mathcal S=(V,E,C,R,\Sigma)
\]

where \(V\) contains narrative objects, \(E\) their explicit relationships, \(C\) hard constraints, \(R\) transformation/repair rules, and \(\Sigma\) the current state. The crucial move is to encode *relationships themselves as first-class objects*, rather than merely storing an outline.

For example, instead of:

```python
protagonist.wound = "past failure"
```

we'd encode something more like:

```python
Relation(
    source="past_failure",
    target="protagonist_vulnerability",
    type="causes",
    strength="necessary"
)

Relation(
    source="protagonist_vulnerability",
    target="attraction_to_catalyst",
    type="enables",
    strength="necessary"
)

Relation(
    source="revelation",
    target="original_desire",
    type="fulfills"
)

Relation(
    source="revelation",
    target="original_desire",
    type="negates"
)
```

That last pair is especially important. **Contradiction can itself be structural information.** We don't want Python deciding that `fulfills` and `negates` are incompatible and collapsing them. Their simultaneous truth is one of the story's structural invariants.

### Then mutation becomes controlled graph rewriting

Suppose we change one thing:

```text
Catalyst relationship:
    romantic → sibling
```

The system doesn't regenerate the story. It asks:

```text
What directly depends on this node?
        ↓
Which relationships are now invalid?
        ↓
Which constraints are violated?
        ↓
Which downstream nodes actually require modification?
        ↓
What must remain untouched?
```

So you'd get something like:

```text
CHANGE
  catalyst_relationship:
      romantic → sibling

INVALIDATED
  sexual_attraction
  romantic_courtship
  erotic_intimacy

STILL VALID
  trust
  fascination
  shared technical language
  emotional vulnerability
  initiation into catalyst's world
  revelation
  betrayal
  fulfills-and-negates-desire structure

REQUIRES REPAIR
  mechanism_of_attraction
  intimacy_sequence
  nature_of_betrayal

PRESERVE
  everything else
```

And **only those three damaged structures become eligible for transformation.**

That gives us serial mutation rather than cascading improvisation.

---

## The more interesting version

I would actually encode the story on several simultaneous layers:

```text
                    STORY STATE
                         │
        ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
        ↓                ↓                ↓
    EVENTS            ENTITIES         WORLD
        │                │                │
        └──────────┬─────┴───────┬────────┘
                   ↓             ↓
              CAUSAL GRAPH   KNOWLEDGE GRAPH
                   │             │
             "X causes Y"   "A knows X but
                            doesn't know Y"
                   │             │
        ┌──────────┴─────────────┘
        ↓
   PSYCHOLOGICAL GRAPH
        │
   desire / fear / guilt /
   attraction / misbelief
        │
        ↓
    THEMATIC GRAPH
        │
   parallels / inversions /
   repetitions / substitutions
        │
        ↓
    SYMBOLIC GRAPH
        │
   object A recalls event B
   event B echoes event C
        │
        ↓
   NARRATIVE GRAPH
        │
   revelation order /
   suspense / callbacks /
   setup → payoff
```

These are **cross-linked rather than independent layers**.

That matters enormously.

For instance, if we mutate an early event, Python can discover that it affects:

\[
\text{Event}
\rightarrow
\text{Memory}
\rightarrow
\text{Guilt}
\rightarrow
\text{Decision}
\rightarrow
\text{Relationship}
\rightarrow
\text{Later Misinterpretation}
\rightarrow
\text{Climax}
\]

while simultaneously participating in:

\[
\text{Event}
\rightarrow
\text{Object/Symbol}
\rightarrow
\text{Loss}
\rightarrow
\text{Replacement}
\rightarrow
\text{Ending Echo}.
\]

Those two chains can intersect without being collapsed into one causal chain.

## And this gives you something rather unusual

We could define **mutation operators** independently of content:

```python
replace(node, new_value)
invert(node)
remove(node)
duplicate(node)
swap(node_a, node_b)
reassign(node, new_owner)
move(event, new_position)
change_relation(a, b, old_relation, new_relation)
```

Then give every mutation a transaction cycle:

```python
candidate = story.copy()

candidate.apply(mutation)

damage = candidate.trace_dependencies()

candidate.repair_required_dependencies()

candidate.validate_hard_constraints()

candidate.validate_chronology()
candidate.validate_knowledge()
candidate.validate_causality()
candidate.validate_motivation()
candidate.validate_setup_payoff()
candidate.validate_thematic_structure()

if candidate.valid:
    commit(candidate)
else:
    rollback()
```

So **randomization doesn't mean statistical generation**.

It can literally mean:

```python
mutation = random.choice(legal_mutations)
```

using Python's pseudorandom generator merely to select among discrete transformations. Every consequence thereafter can be deterministic.

Even better, we can distinguish:

```text
HARD INVARIANTS
Cannot break.

SOFT INVARIANTS
May break, but must be reported.

DERIVED FACTS
Recalculate automatically.

DEPENDENT STRUCTURES
Repair explicitly.

FREE VARIABLES
Can change without repair.

LOCKED VARIABLES
Cannot change during this experiment.
```

That gives you a genuinely useful experimental instrument.

You could say:

> Change exactly **one** structurally legal thing at random.

Run it.

Then:

> Preserve that state. Change another.

Run it again.

And eventually you get a **mutation lineage**:

```text
S₀
│
├─ Δ1: relationship transformed
↓
S₁
│
├─ Δ2: setting transformed
↓
S₂
│
├─ Δ3: revelation moved earlier
↓
S₃
│
├─ Δ4: protagonist/catalyst knowledge asymmetry inverted
↓
S₄
```

Each \(S_n\) is completely inspectable, and every difference from \(S_0\) has provenance.

You can therefore ask much more interesting questions than "generate another story like this":

**How far can I transform this narrative before its structural identity disappears?**

Or lock the deep structure and deliberately obliterate everything superficial:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Maximum surface difference}
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\text{structural isomorphism}
}
\]

That's particularly interesting here because the skeleton we extracted isn't merely an act sequence. It contains **recursive dependencies, delayed information, mistaken interpretations, mirrored events, substitutions, reversals, and setup/payoff relationships**. Those are exactly the things a graph-and-constraint representation can preserve without having to approximate them statistically.

And I would go one step further than my previous abstraction: **encode the actual story first at high resolution, then derive the reusable skeleton computationally from it.** That prevents us from losing fine structure because *we* decided in advance what counted as important.

We could build the first Python implementation directly against the complete uploaded text: scene → beat → event → state change → dependency → cross-layer relationship, with validators and a single-mutation engine.
